title: Study Smarter: Active Recall and Spacing
subject: careers

sections.body: Re-reading notes and highlighting feel productive but are among the least effective ways to study.

Active recall (the testing effect): close the book and pull information out of memory with flashcards, practice questions, or explaining it aloud. Retrieval strengthens memory more than re-reading does.
Spaced repetition (the spacing effect): review material over increasing gaps (1 day, 3 days, a week) instead of cramming it all at once.
Interleaving: mix different types of problems in one session, so you learn to choose the right method, not just repeat one.
Honest Learn brings finished lessons back for review after a few days. That's spaced repetition built in.
Turn today's notes from any subject into 5 questions. Answer them tomorrow without looking, then again in 3 days.

quiz.q: You have an exam in two weeks. Which plan uses the spacing effect?
options: Short sessions spread across the two weeks
hints: Spacing is about WHEN you study.
Cramming puts all the study in one block.
Example: practising piano 20 minutes a day beats 3 hours once a week.
quiz.explain: Spreading study over time with gaps beats cramming for long-term memory.

hints: Active recall means pulling information OUT of memory.
Which one works without looking at the material?
Example: explaining a topic to a friend from memory is active recall.
quiz.explain: Answering without notes forces retrieval, which strengthens memory.

quiz.q: Why does mixing problem types (interleaving) help?
options: You practise choosing the right method
hints: What do exams usually do with problem types?
In a block of identical problems, do you ever choose a method?
Example: a footballer who only practises penalties may struggle in a real match where situations vary.
quiz.explain: Mixed practice trains you to recognise which method each problem needs, just like in an exam.
